new_statements.quote: [5.1] HC is now largely monosyllabic, although forms with more than one syllable occur. In contrast, the earliest Proto-Chamic (PC) forms were overwhelmingly disyllabic. It can be argued that the tendency toward monosyllabification began at the PC level with the switch from initial to final stress in disyllabic forms. [...] [5.5] All synchronic analyses of HC agree that it has five phonemic tones [...] [1.2] In terms of phonology, HC has restructured from a sesquisyllabic, iambically stressed, atonal (although probably marginally registral) language to a monosyllabic, fully tonal language. New phonemes have also been added under the influence of the languages of Hainan.
new_statements.citation: Thurgood, Graham, Ela Thurgood & Li Fengxiang. 2014. A Grammatical Sketch of Hainan Cham: History, Contact, and Phonology (Pacific Linguistics 643). Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter Mouton. ISBN 978-1-61451-604-0, DOI 10.1515/9781614516040.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files checked under ( present, 10 saved sources + Google Books preview folder). (1) Verbatim check: I viewed the page images and of Thurgood, Thurgood & Li 2014 (Google Books preview, id fSgABwAAQBAJ) and the scanned of PT50/PT51. PT47 shows 'Chapter 5 The Hainan Cham sound system... 5.1 Word structure: HC is now largely monosyllabic, although forms with more than one syllable occur. In contrast, the earliest Proto-Chamic (PC) forms were overwhelmingly disyllabic. It can be argued that the tendency toward monosyllabification began at the PC level with the switch from initial to final stress in disyllabic forms.' -- exactly as quoted. PT50 sec. 5.5: 'All synchronic analyses of HC agree that…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Modern Tsat/Hainan Cham is a largely monosyllabic, fully tonal language with five phonemic tones (55, 33, 21, 43, 24); the grammar makes no synchronic word-stress statement. Stress figures only in the history: Proto-Malayo-Chamic penultimate stress > Proto-Chamic final (iambic) stress > loss of the presyllable > Tsat monosyllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Polysyllabic forms exist (mostly loans/compounds) but no prominence pattern is described for them; sec. 5.5 notes limited tone sandhi (three examples from Ouyang & Zheng 1983: 32-33), two classifiers whose 55 tone varies with 21, and that 'final particles often have a neutral tone rather than their basic tone'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/syllable level (lexical tone on every syllable; citation forms). Phrase-level focus prosody is treated separately by Wang et al. 2012 (no post-focus compression).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same variety: Tsat = Hainan Cham (HC) = Utsat = Huihui(hua) 回辉话, spoken in Huihui and Huixin villages, Yanglan township, Sanya, Hainan (Glottolog tsat1238, ISO huq). The 2014 grammar and the 2005 chapter rest on Zheng 1997 plus the authors' 2004 fieldwork (6 speakers).

sources.quote: [5.1] HC is now largely monosyllabic, although forms with more than one syllable occur. In contrast, the earliest Proto-Chamic (PC) forms were overwhelmingly disyllabic. It can be argued that the tendency toward monosyllabification began at the PC level with the switch from initial to final stress in disyllabic forms. [...] [5.5] All synchronic analyses of HC agree that it has five phonemic tones [...] [1.2] In terms of phonology, HC has restructured from a sesquisyllabic, iambically stressed, atonal (although probably marginally registral) language to a monosyllabic, fully tonal language. sources.locator: Ch. 5 'The Hainan Cham sound system', sec. 5.1 Word structure (print p. 36; Google Books ebook page PT47) and sec. 5.5 Tones (PT50); ch. 1 sec. 1.2 'Convergence Under Contact' (PT24)
sources.note: Synchronic HC is 'largely monosyllabic' and 'fully tonal' with five phonemic tones (55, 33, 21, 43, 24); stress is mentioned only diachronically: HC 'restructured from a sesquisyllabic, iambically stressed, atonal... language to a monosyllabic, fully tonal language'; PC 'switch from initial to final stress'. No synchronic word-stress statement; notes tone sandhi (3 examples) and that final particles often carry a neutral tone.

sources.citation: Thurgood, Graham & Li Fengxiang. 2007. From Malayic to Sinitic: the restructuring of Tsat [Hainan Cham] under intense contact. In Wayland, Hartmann & Sidwell (eds), SEALS XII (2002), 133-140. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics
sources.note: pp.133-134: 'Malayo-Chamic had penultimate stress... stress switched to final position'; PC sesquisyllabic 'in terms of stress, iambic'; Tsat then became monosyllabic and tonal. Diachronic.

sources.citation: Thurgood, Graham. 2006 ms [publ. 2010, Journal of Language Contact VARIA 3: 39-65]. Hainan Cham, Anong, and Phan Rang Cham: three languages, three social contexts, three patterns of change (Kobe conference paper)
sources.note: Sec. 2.1.1: on arrival in Hainan 'it was sesquisyllabic - a weakly stressed onset syllable followed by a stressed main syllable; under the influence of the tonal languages of Hainan, it became monosyllabic and tonal - Modern Hainan Cham has a rich, 5-way tonal system'.

sources.citation: Norquest, Peter. 2005. Word structure in Chamic: prosodic alignment versus segmental faithfulness. In Chamic and Beyond, 147-188 (PL 569). hdl 1885/254227
sources.note: Sec. 3.3 (pp.180-182): Tsat moved to Hainan 'where monosyllabic, fully tonal languages... are the norm'; 'rapid reduction of the prosodic word in which unstressed syllables were simply deleted'. Diachronic prosody only.

sources.citation: Thurgood, Graham. 1996. Language contact and the directionality of internal drift: the development of tones and registers in Chamic. Language 72(1): 1-31 [author preprint 'Chamic contact', 44 pp.]
sources.note: Sec. 2: final stress introduced into PC under Mon-Khmer influence produced iambic words; languages 'such as Tsat, have reduced almost all disyllables to monosyllables'; sec. 6 Tsat tones. Diachronic only.

sources.citation: Thurgood, Graham. 1992. From atonal to tonal in Utsat (a Chamic language of Hainan). BLS 18 (Special Session on the Typology of Tone Languages), 145-156. DOI 10.3765/bls.v18i2.1535
sources.note: Sec. 3.0: 'Under the influence of the mainland Austroasiatic forms, stress came to rest on the final syllable, leaving the pre-syllable unstressed and subsequently, this unstressed vowel dropped'; Utsat 'has become monosyllabic and fully tonal'. Diachronic.

sources.citation: Fan Zhiquan, Fu Peipei & Ye Yunong. 2025. The typology conversion and integration history of Tsat and Utsat in Sanya, Hainan. Advances in Linguistics Research 7(4): 235-248. DOI 10.35534/lin.0704024
sources.note: Sociolinguistic/typological overview: 'monosyllabic words, the use of tones to differentiate word meanings'; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Wang Bei, Li Chenxia, Wu Qian, Zhang Xiaxia, Wang Baofeng & Xu Yi. 2012. Production and perception of focus in PFC and non-PFC languages: comparing Beijing Mandarin and Hainan Tsat. Interspeech 2012. DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2012-204
sources.note: Instrumental focus-prosody study (phrase level): Tsat 'has developed into a full-fledge tone language'; focus marked by duration, no post-focus compression. Nothing on word stress.

sources.citation: Grant, Anthony P. 2005. The effects of intimate multidirectional linguistic contact in Chamic. In Chamic and Beyond, 37-104 (PL 569). hdl 1885/254231
sources.note: Mentions the five-tone system of Tsat vs six tones of Hainanese; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Thurgood, Graham & Ela Thurgood. 2005. The tones from Proto-Chamic to Tsat [Hainan Cham]: insights from Zheng 1997 and summer 2004 fieldwork. In Grant & Sidwell (eds), Chamic and Beyond, 247-271. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics (PL 569). DOI 10.15144/PL-569.247
sources.note: p.249: 'Contact with the iambic Austroasiatic patterned languages... caused a switch in stress from penultimate to iambic, ultimately resulting in a reduction first to iambic and then to monosyllabic Chamic forms'; p.251: 'All analyses of Tsat treat the language as essentially having five phonemic tones'. Instrumental tone study (6 speakers); no synchronic stress statement.
